prompt: Randomised quicksort always returns a correctly sorted array, but its running time depends on its random pivot choices. What kind of randomised algorithm is it?

options.explanation: Monte Carlo algorithms have a running-time bound but may err; they need not take exactly the same time on every run.
Correct. With distinct keys and uniform random pivots, expected time is O(n log n) for every fixed input of n keys; unlucky runs taking O(n²) remain possible.
Its pivot choices come from random bits, so its behaviour on a fixed input varies between runs.

BPP names a class of yes/no decision problems, while the prompt asks for a kind of sorting algorithm. Always-correct random running time is the Las Vegas property; decision problems with expected-polynomial-time algorithms of that kind form ZPP.

workedExample: Separate correctness from runtime. Random pivots change the search work, but not whether quicksort sorts correctly. That is Las Vegas behaviour. A fixed number of Miller–Rabin rounds instead has a running-time bound while permitting a false ‘probably prime’ answer. Expectations and errors are over the algorithm’s random choices for each fixed input.

prompt: A problem has two algorithms: R, an RP algorithm (never accepts no-instances; accepts yes-instances with probability at least 1/2), and C, a coRP algorithm (never rejects yes-instances; rejects no-instances with probability at least 1/2). With fresh independent randomness each round, you repeat "run R; if it accepts, answer yes. Run C; if it rejects, answer no." until you get an answer. Which is true?

options.text: It sometimes gives the wrong answer, so it's a BPP algorithm
options.explanation: Every answer it gives is certain: R accepting proves yes, C rejecting proves no. It never errs.

options.text: It never errs and needs at most 2 rounds in expectation, so the problem is in ZPP
options.explanation: Correct. Each round answers with probability at least 1/2 (on a yes-instance R accepts at least half the time; on a no-instance C rejects at least half the time), so the expected number of rounds is at most 2.

options.text: It may loop forever, so it's not a valid algorithm
options.explanation: With fresh independent rounds the probability of never stopping is zero and expected runtime is polynomial. ZPP does not require a finite worst-case time bound over all random sequences.

options.text: It shows the problem is in P
options.explanation: Expected polynomial time with randomness gives ZPP. Whether ZPP equals P is open (conjectured).

workedExample: RP acceptance is conclusive evidence of yes; coRP rejection is conclusive evidence of no. Running both and stopping only on those outcomes never gives an incorrect answer. On each input, a round stops with probability at least one half, so fresh independent rounds take at most two rounds on average. Expected polynomial time gives ZPP without a fixed worst-case stopping time.
